Osteoporosis: an age-related disorder characterised by decreased bone mass and increased chances of fractures; decreased levels of estrogen is a common cause, so it is frequent in women after menopause.

Gout: inflammation of joints due to accumulation of uric acid crystals, often in the joint of the big toe.

pyq.q:
Two athletes train for a school meet: Priya runs the 100 m sprint and Amit runs the 5 km race. Priya's coach notes that her leg muscles produce very powerful, rapid contractions but tire within seconds, while Amit can keep a steady pace for half an hour. A biopsy would show that the muscles of the two athletes differ in the amount of a red pigment, in the number of mitochondria and in the amount of sarcoplasmic reticulum.
(i) Name the red pigment and state its function.
(ii) Which type of muscle fibre predominates in Priya's sprint muscles and in Amit's endurance muscles?
(iii) Explain why Priya's muscles tire within seconds.
(iv) Which athlete's fibres have more sarcoplasmic reticulum, and why is that useful?
pyq.answer:
(i) Myoglobin, an oxygen-storing pigment in muscle that holds a reserve of O2 for the mitochondria.

(ii) Priya: white fibres (little myoglobin, few mitochondria, anaerobic). Amit: red fibres (much myoglobin, many mitochondria, aerobic).

(iii) White fibres depend on the anaerobic breakdown of glycogen for ATP; repeated activation makes lactic acid accumulate in them quickly, causing fatigue.

(iv) Priya's white fibres have more sarcoplasmic reticulum. A larger store of Ca2+ can be released and pumped back faster, allowing the rapid, powerful contractions a sprint needs.

pyq.q:
A 68-year-old woman slips in her bathroom and fractures the neck of her femur. The doctor tells the family that her bones have lost mass over the years since her menopause, that the joint involved is the one where the head of the femur fits into a cup of the hip bone, and that this cup is formed where three bones fused during childhood.
(i) Name the disorder that made the fracture likely and give its common cause.
(ii) Name the cup and the three bones that fuse to form it.
(iii) What type of joint is the hip joint? Name one other joint of the same type.
(iv) Name the girdle involved and state how its two halves meet in the midline.
pyq.answer:
(i) Osteoporosis: an age-related disorder with decreased bone mass and increased chances of fractures; decreased estrogen level after menopause is a common cause.

(ii) The acetabulum; it lies at the point of fusion of the ilium, ischium and pubis, which together form the coxal bone.

(iii) A ball and socket synovial joint; the shoulder joint between the head of the humerus and the glenoid cavity is another.

(iv) The pelvic girdle, made of two coxal bones; the two halves meet ventrally at the pubic symphysis, which contains fibrous cartilage.

pyq.q:
An electron micrograph of a resting sarcomere shows a dark band 1.6 μm long with a paler central region 0.4 μm wide, flanked on each side by a light band, the Z lines being 2.4 μm apart. After the muscle is stimulated the Z lines are found 2.0 μm apart.
(i) Name the dark band, the paler central region and the light band.
(ii) What is the length of the dark band after contraction? Justify.
(iii) What happens to the paler central region and the light bands on contraction?
(iv) Which ion and which protein on the thin filament made the contraction possible?
pyq.answer:
(i) The dark band is the A band (anisotropic); the paler central region is the H zone; the light band is the I band (isotropic).

(ii) Still 1.6 μm. The A band is the length of the thick myosin filaments, and the filaments do not shorten; the thin filaments slide over them.

(iii) Both shorten. The thin filaments slide 0.2 μm inwards from each side, so the H zone (thick filaments only) narrows from 0.4 μm to zero and each I band (thin filaments only) shortens from 0.4 μm to 0.2 μm; the two I bands together lose 0.4 μm, which matches the Z lines moving from 2.4 to 2.0 μm.

(iv) Ca2+ released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum binds to a subunit of troponin, unmasking the active sites on actin so that myosin heads can form cross bridges.

practice_mcq.q: Which cells of the human body show amoeboid movement?
options: Ciliated epithelial cells of the trachea
practice_mcq.explanation: Macrophages and leucocytes move by pseudopodia formed through streaming of protoplasm, helped by microfilaments. Sperm move by a flagellum.

practice_mcq.q: The passage of ova through the female reproductive tract is facilitated by
practice_mcq.explanation: The fallopian tube is lined with ciliated epithelium whose coordinated beating moves the ovum; the ovum has no flagellum.

practice_mcq.q: Muscle tissue is derived from which embryonic germ layer, and what fraction of adult body weight does it make up?
practice_mcq.explanation: NCERT: muscle is a specialised tissue of mesodermal origin and about 40 to 50 per cent of the body weight of an adult human is contributed by muscles.

practice_mcq.q: The light band of a myofibril is called the
options: A band, because it contains actin
I band, because it is isotropic and contains actin
H zone, because it contains myosin only
M line, because it holds the myosin filaments
practice_mcq.explanation: The light band contains actin and is the I (isotropic) band; the dark A (anisotropic) band contains myosin.

practice_mcq.q: The Z line
options: Bisects the A band and holds the thick filaments
Bisects the I band and anchors the thin filaments
Lies in the centre of the H zone
Is the plasma membrane of the muscle fibre
practice_mcq.explanation: The Z line is an elastic fibre in the centre of each I band to which the thin filaments are firmly attached; the M line holds the thick filaments at the centre of the A band.

practice_mcq.q: Each F actin is a polymer of
practice_mcq.explanation: F (filamentous) actin is a polymer of monomeric G (globular) actin; two F actins wind helically to form the thin filament.

practice_mcq.q: The cross arm of a thick filament consists of
options: The globular head and short arm of meromyosin (HMM)
practice_mcq.explanation: The heavy meromyosin, the head with its short arm, projects outwards from the filament surface and is called the cross arm; the tail is light meromyosin.

practice_mcq.q: In the resting muscle the active sites for myosin on actin are masked by
practice_mcq.explanation: NCERT wording: in the resting state a subunit of troponin masks the active binding sites for myosin on the actin filaments; Ca<sup>2+</sup> binding to troponin removes the mask.

practice_mcq.q: Immediately after the myosin head completes its pull on actin it
options: Binds a new ATP and the cross bridge breaks
Releases ADP and P<sub>i</sub> and returns to the relaxed state
Pumps Ca<sup>2+</sup> back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum
practice_mcq.explanation: After the pull, myosin releases ADP and P<sub>i</sub> and goes back to its relaxed state; only then does a new ATP bind and break the cross bridge.

practice_mcq.q: Relaxation of a contracted muscle fibre occurs when
options: Acetylcholine is released at the motor end plate
Ca<sup>2+</sup> is pumped back into the sarcoplasmic cisternae
practice_mcq.explanation: When Ca<sup>2+</sup> returns to the sarcoplasmic reticulum, troponin masks the actin sites again and the Z lines go back to their original positions.

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following is a set of true ribs?
practice_mcq.explanation: The first seven pairs attach dorsally to the thoracic vertebrae and ventrally to the sternum by hyaline cartilage; 8 to 10 are vertebrochondral, 11 and 12 floating.

practice_mcq.q: Number of cervical vertebrae in a giraffe is
practice_mcq.explanation: The number of cervical vertebrae is seven in almost all mammals, whatever the length of the neck.

practice_mcq.q: The depression on the scapula that receives the head of the humerus is the
practice_mcq.explanation: The glenoid cavity lies below the acromion and forms the shoulder joint with the humerus; the acetabulum is the corresponding cavity of the pelvic girdle.

practice_mcq.q: The number of tarsals and carpals respectively in one hind limb and one forelimb is
practice_mcq.explanation: Tarsals (ankle) are 7 and carpals (wrist) are 8; metatarsals and metacarpals are 5 each; phalanges 14 each.

practice_mcq.q: The joint between adjacent vertebrae is a
practice_mcq.explanation: Adjacent vertebrae are joined by cartilage (the intervertebral disc), a cartilaginous joint permitting limited movement.

practice_mcq.q: The saddle joint is found between the
options: Carpal and metacarpal of the thumb
practice_mcq.explanation: The saddle joint at the base of the thumb allows movement in two planes; atlas–axis is pivot, shoulder and hip are ball and socket.

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following joints allows no movement?
practice_mcq.explanation: Fibrous joints such as the sutures of the skull are immovable; cartilaginous joints allow limited movement and synovial joints considerable movement.

practice_mcq.q: Tetany results from
options: Autoimmune damage to the neuromuscular junction
practice_mcq.explanation: Tetany is rapid spasms of muscle due to low Ca<sup>2+</sup> in body fluid; the autoimmune junction disorder is myasthenia gravis.

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following is NOT a disorder of the muscular or skeletal system?
practice_mcq.explanation: Atherosclerosis is a disorder of the arteries (fat deposits narrowing the lumen), from the circulation chapter; the other three are from this chapter.

practice_mcq.q: The two halves of the pelvic girdle meet ventrally at the
practice_mcq.explanation: The pubic symphysis, containing fibrous cartilage, is where the two coxal bones meet in the ventral midline; the sacrum lies between them dorsally.

common_mistakes: Writing that the A band shortens during contraction. The A band equals the length of the thick filaments and stays constant; the I band and the H zone shorten. This single line decides a mark in nearly every paper.
Saying that the filaments shorten. In the sliding filament theory neither actin nor myosin changes length; the sarcomere shortens because the overlap increases. Use the word 'slide' in the answer.
Confusing troponin with tropomyosin. In NCERT wording it is a subunit of troponin that masks the active sites on actin at rest and that binds Ca<sup>2+</sup>; tropomyosin is the strand it sits on.

Calling cardiac muscle non-striated. Cardiac muscle is striated and involuntary; only visceral (smooth) muscle is non-striated. Similarly, the muscles of the alimentary canal are smooth, not striated.

Getting the bone counts wrong: 12 pairs of ribs (not 11), 8 cranial and 14 facial bones, 7 cervical vertebrae, 8 carpals but 7 tarsals, 14 phalanges per limb, 30 bones per limb, 26 vertebrae (not 33; the sacral and coccygeal vertebrae are counted as one each because they are fused).

Mixing up the sockets and the girdles: the glenoid cavity is on the scapula (pectoral) for the humerus, the acetabulum is on the coxal bone (pelvic) for the femur. The acromion is a process of the scapula, not a cavity.

Naming the joint without its class. Exercise 9 wants 'fibrous joint' for cranial bones and 'cartilaginous joint' for the pubic symphysis; writing 'gliding' or 'hinge' for those is wrong because they are not synovial.

Attributing red fibres to anaerobic respiration or giving white fibres the higher myoglobin. Red = myoglobin rich, mitochondria rich, aerobic, slow to fatigue; white = the reverse but with more sarcoplasmic reticulum.
Writing lactic acid for gout or uric acid for fatigue. Gout is uric acid crystals in joints; fatigue is lactic acid from anaerobic breakdown of glycogen in muscle. And tetany is not tetanus.

Drawing the sarcomere without the H zone and M line, or placing the Z line in the A band. The Z line bisects the I band and bounds the sarcomere; the M line and H zone sit in the centre of the A band.
strategy:
This chapter is two lists and one mechanism, so split your time that way. Spend the first sitting on the muscle half: draw the sarcomere from memory until you can label Z line, A band, I band, H zone and M line without looking, then write the sliding filament theory as eight numbered steps and check each against NCERT. Draw the thin filament (two F actins, tropomyosin, troponin) and the meromyosin unit (head, short arm, tail, ATPase) once each. Those three drawings plus the steps are the 5-mark question in almost every school final and the source of the standard NEET question.

Spend the second sitting on the skeleton. Memorise the numbers as sums, not as isolated facts: 80 axial = 22 + 1 + 6 + 26 + 1 + 24, and 126 appendicular = 4 × 30 + 4 + 2, with the 30 of each limb broken into its five parts. Then learn the six sites of exercise 9 with the type and class of joint at each, and the six disorders as one-line definitions with the key word in each.

For the 3-mark 'differentiate' questions (skeletal, visceral and cardiac muscle; actin and myosin; red and white fibres; pectoral and pelvic girdle) prepare a table of four or five rows each; the examiner marks rows, not paragraphs. In the paper, draw every diagram in pencil with ruled label lines and give each diagram a title. If a question says 'describe', write in steps or bullet points so that the marking points stand out. Ten minutes of the night before the exam should go to reciting the bone counts and the joint sites; the rest of this chapter rewards understanding the mechanism, which does not need cramming once the drawings are in your hand.
